routeDescription: Aylesbeare Common is a quieter, wilder walk for children who enjoy nature spotting more than play equipment. There are two signed trails — a short 0.75-mile route and a longer 3-mile route — with heathland, birds, butterflies, dragonflies and seasonal colour. Heath spotted orchids and bog plants like sundew add to the nature interest, and the hilltop position gives lovely views from either side of the reserve. The longer trail can be uneven, with gradients, steps and gates, so choose the shorter or tarmac farm-track option across the road from the main car park if legs are small and tire quickly. routeDescription: The Beer to Branscombe route follows the South West Coast Path across cliff tops and through woodland, with wide sea views and Branscombe giving the walk a clear destination. The outward section from Beer climbs to Beer Head before dropping via 83 steps down to Branscombe Mouth, so legs need to be willing as this is not a flat or gentle walk. The return via the Hooken Undercliff is one of the more dramatic stretches of the Jurassic Coast: a ten-acre landslip that broke away from the cliff in 1790, leaving chalk pinnacles and a mysterious tangled wilderness that children tend to find properly interesting. Branscombe has pubs, a National Trust tea room and a working forge to pause at, and the 899 bus runs back to Beer if legs give out at the end. Note that as of early 2026, one section of the coast path near the Hooken was subject to a closure due to subsidence, so it's worth check the South West Coast Path website before visiting.

routeDescription: Denbury Hillfort is a Scheduled Ancient Monument near Newton Abbot, sitting on top of Denbury Down and dating to around 300–100BC. The hillfort is unusually well preserved, with impressive double ramparts and deep ditches on the south and east sides, and two Bronze Age burial mounds inside the fort interior that predate the Iron Age structure itself. Access is via a short ten-minute walk up a lane from the village — narrow and hedged with wildflowers in spring — and the site has interpretation boards explaining what you're looking at. Children can walk the full circumference along the outer ditch path, which takes about twenty minutes and gives a real sense of the scale of the earthworks. In spring the woodland floor inside the fort fills with bluebells. Local legend says a golden crown is buried somewhere on Denbury Down, which is a fun detail mentioning to children before you set off to add an extra spark to the trip.

With the café, toilets, second-hand bookshop and shop all at the main visitor hub, it's one of the easier full-day outdoor options in East Devon, particularly if you're already a National Trust member.

routeDescription: A rewarding Jurassic Coast walk for families with older children who enjoy a proper adventure, combining woodland paths, hillside climbs and sweeping views across Lyme Bay. routeDescription: This circular walk has a darker Dartmoor edge, linking Cadover Bridge with the wooded Dewerstone valley and the granite crags of Dewerstone Rock. The route moves from open moorland into ancient oak woodland, with rivers, boulders, quarry remains and dramatic rock faces along the way. The Dewerstone is wrapped in local folklore: its name is linked with “Dewer”, a devil-like huntsman said to ride across the moor with ghostly Wisht Hounds, luring lost travellers towards the crags. That legend gives the walk a more atmospheric feel for older children, especially once the woodland closes in and the rock rises above the valley. It is a more demanding family walk than the short Dewerstone Wood loop, with uneven, muddy and steeper sections, but the mix of open moor, river, crags, woodland and folklore makes it feel like a proper Dartmoor expedition.

routeDescription: Dewerstone has more drama than a gentle woodland walk: deep wooded valley, big granite crags, old quarry remains, the River Plym and the River Meavy meeting near Shaugh Bridge, and climbers often visible on the rock faces. For families, the easiest route is the National Trust’s short Dewerstone Wood circular, which follows the river, crosses footbridges and passes traces of the old granite tramway without needing to climb high onto the crags. Children who like boulders, rivers, bridges, ruins and “wild” woods will probably get more from it than those who need a clear destination as it's more of an explore along a route with lots to look at. There are longer, steeper routes from Cadover Bridge or Shaugh Bridge that bring in moorland views and Dewerstone Rock itself, but those feel more like proper Dartmoor walks and need more care with edges, mud and tired legs.

routeDescription: Avon Reservoir is one of the more manageable ways to get a proper Dartmoor feeling without committing to a difficult moorland route. From Shipley Bridge, the walk follows the River Avon gradually uphill towards the dam, moving from wooded valley and riverside sections into more open moorland as the reservoir comes into view. The tarmac track makes the main route unusually straightforward for Dartmoor, while the scale of the dam, the sound of the river and the shift into wilder scenery give children enough to notice along the way. It is a good one for families who want water, moorland and a sense of reaching somewhere, without needing a long or technical walk. The route can be made slightly longer or shorter depending on the turnaround point, extending the route to 7 miles if you wish. The terrain is mostly tarmac, so it can work for bikes and scooters if you're willing to bump or carry them for the final stretch of rocky gravel. The toilets here are public toilets, and are not open 24/7, and there's occasionally a coffee van in the car park if you're in luck!

routeDescription: Meldon Reservoir sits below some of Dartmoor’s higher ground, with the dam, dark water, West Okement Valley and Meldon Viaduct all close enough to give the place a strong sense of landscape without needing a long moorland walk. The shorter route is useful for a contained reservoir stop, while older or more confident walkers can use Meldon as a starting point for a much more substantial Dartmoor outing. routeDescription: Tottiford and Trenchford sit quietly within a wooded Dartmoor valley, with linked paths running between the water, trees, footbridges and old reservoir structures. The walk has a peaceful, slightly hidden feel: still water through the branches, birds moving across the reeds, small bridges to cross and enough changes in the path to make it feel more interesting than a simple lakeside loop. Tottiford has the more rugged round-reservoir feel, while Trenchford adds quieter woodland and open water views nearby. Together, they create a gentle but satisfying reservoir walk, with small milestones for younger children and enough distance and variety for older kids. Not buggy friendly with lots of roots and uneven ground, so it's one for the backcarrier if you've got very young children with you, but it's a nice, quieter spot with plenty of shade and a few places where you could paddle close to the waters edge at Trenchford that work well on a sunny day.

routeDescription: Squabmoor Reservoir sits on Woodbury Common within the East Devon Pebblebed Heaths, with water, woodland, heathland paths and fishing spots giving it a quieter, more tucked-away feel than the larger family reservoirs. routeName: Granite Way: Okehampton to Meldon Reservoir
routeDescription: The Granite Way from Okehampton towards Meldon follows the old railway line out of town, giving families a mostly traffic-free route with wide Dartmoor views through hedgerows, the occasional view of railway heritage (old, disused stations and lines) and the landmark crossing of Meldon Viaduct. The full Granite Way continues on towards Lydford, but this shorter section gives a clear destination without needing to take on the whole trail. The viaduct is the main moment of the route, with views across Meldon Dam, the reservoir, quarry landscape and open moorland beyond. From the viaduct, you can link down towards Meldon Reservoir for a waterside pause and picnic stop before turning back. The surface (mostly stone track) and gradient (almost entirely flat except a few small inclines) make it more manageable than many Dartmoor routes, but there are still a few steeper sections, shared-use sections and open, exposed stretches where weather changes the feel of the route. It's not the peaceful route it's sometimes painted as; you can hear the road from all points, and the scenery is beautiful but the brambles and hedgerows do make this something to glance (and through) at rather than wide open scenic views. The Viaduct is the an impressive feature to incentivise the route, and, if legs tire on the return journey there is a small cafe at the Station Car park that sell a good selection of fresh cakes and snacks.

routeDescription: This shorter section of the Wray Valley Trail gives families an easy way onto the old railway line without committing to the full Bovey-to-Moretonhampstead route; naturally you can extend the route as far as Moretonhampstead if you choose for older riders, but it's adaptability makes it workable for mixed energy levels or deciding on the day. From Bovey Tracey the best start point is from within the Park, the trail leads towards Parke and follows the River Bovey into the National Trust estate, with woodland, riverside glimpses and the sense of moving from town into countryside quite quickly. From the trail itself you can't actually see the river until you arrive on the edge of the Parke Estate. It's worth noting that there are multiple entry-points into the Parke Estate from the trail, but all involve a steep slope; it's passable for bikes, but it's worth bearing in mind that you don't cycle along the river, nor can you see it from this section of the track; it's very much a woodland ride. The wider Wray Valley Trail is a 7-mile mainly traffic-free route from Bovey Tracey to Moretonhampstead which does bring you closer to the river, but this Bovey-to-Parke stretch works as a smaller walk, scooter ride or cycle when you want a contained outing with a clear pause point at Parke. To get to the cafe (Home Cafe) at Parke, you'll need to climb a fairly steep hill; another factor worth considering if you're riding with littler legs. The railway-line surface and shared-use path make it a manageable route for less experienced riders, and if you're willing to bump along through the paths to get to the river, there are countless ideal spots and mini-river beaches well-suited to a picnic spot.
